14.
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law MACT No. 1979/16 Khaitun Nesa & Ors. Vs. Kanchan Yadav &

sentences.text: In the present case, the petitioners have examined the wife of deceased as PW-1 apart from examining an eye witness of the incident being their star witness as PW-2.
The latter has explained the entire sequence of events leading to the death of the deceased victim on account of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver i.e. R1.

The PW2 has clarified the events further during his cross-examination and he has specifically deposed that the offending vehicle was a dumper truck which was unloading sand/debris at the spot of the accident.

The PW2 has deposed that while unloading the debris, the upper part of the offending vehicle came in the contact of overhead electric wire, due to which the circuit got complete and electric current passed throughout the offending vehicle which culminated in the burst of its right front tyre.
The PW2 has deposed that the deceased victim was passing by the side of the offending vehicle when the right side wheel after getting burst came off and hit the deceased.
The PW2 has even deposed during his cross-examination that the rubber portion of the tyre as well as its ring got detached from the wheel.
The fact that the offending vehicle touched the overhead electric wire is also admitted by R1 while deposing as R1W1.

The respondent no. 1 has specifically admitted during his cross-examination that the overhead electric wire was not broken and had not fallen down and that the electricity wire was 2-3 feets above the upper level of his dumper.

The fact that the respondent no. 1 was rash and negligent is duly established on the basis of the testimony of PW2, wherein he has deposed that the R1 was sitting alone MACT No. 1979/16 Khaitun Nesa & Ors. Vs. Kanchan Yadav & Ors.

16. One another defence raised by insurance company is that the victim died due to electrocution and not due to driving of the offending vehicle.

Herein, it is pertinent to note that the claim for compensation as provided under Section 140 & 165 of M.V. Act, 1988 is in respect of accidents involving the death of, or bodily injury to, persons arising out of the "use" of motor vehicles and not due to mere driving on the road only.

The position of the law has also been made clear in case titled as "Babu Vs. Remesan, AIR 1996 Ker 95, wherein it has been held that:-
(iv) In sub-section (1) of section 140 the expression employed by the Legislature is "accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle" in the place of "accident caused by the use of a motor vehicle".
Evidently the Legislature wanted to enlarge the scope of the word 'use' and not to restrict it for denying compensation in deserving cases.
The test should be whether the accident was reasonably proximate to the use of a motor vehicle, whether or not the motor MACT No. 1979/16 Khaitun Nesa & Ors. Vs. Kanchan Yadav & Ors.

It is apparent on perusal of the case file that the death of the victim has been caused due to the use of motor vehicle by R1 in a rash and negligent manner and not due to electrocution.
Hence, the defence contention raised in this regard is hereby rejected.

17. Moreover, the very fact that R-1 has already been specifically arrayed as an accused in case FIR no. 153/16, PS Loni Border, Ghaziabad, for the offences u/s 279/304-A IPC, is itself a strong circumstance to support the above said testimony of PW1 & PW-2 on these issues.

The copies of FIR,
Site plan, seizure memos, mechanical inspection, notice u/s 133 MV Act and charge sheet u/s 173 Cr.PC also corroborate the oral testimony of PW-1 & PW2.
